You are implementing part of an original, from-scratch C re-implementation of the
command-line audio tool at /workspace/executable (self-identifies as "SoX v14.4.2").

CRITICAL RULES (violating these fails the whole project):
 - Learn behaviour ONLY by RUNNING /workspace/executable and reading the bundled
   man pages: /workspace/soxformat.7 (the authority on formats -- READ THE
   SECTIONS FOR YOUR FORMATS), /workspace/sox.1, /workspace/libsox.3, README.md.
 - NEVER search the web, fetch/clone/download upstream source, use a package
   manager to obtain the project, or read any copy of the original sources.
 - NEVER run objdump/gdb/ghidra/strace/ltrace/nm/readelf/strings on the binary.
 - Write ORIGINAL code; derive behaviour from experiments and from the manual.

Read FIRST: /workspace/notes/CONTRACT.md, /workspace/src/sox.h, /workspace/src/sox_i.h.
sox.h/sox_i.h are the fixed contract: you may ADD declarations, never change or
remove existing ones (other agents compile against them concurrently).

ONLY create/modify the files assigned to you, plus a notes file you own.
Never run 'git' write commands.

The project does not link yet, so you CANNOT run an end-to-end comparison.
Therefore: probe the reference exhaustively, record the observed BYTES, work out
the layout, implement, and compile-check every file:
    cc -c -std=gnu99 -I/workspace/src -O2 -Wall /workspace/src/FILE.c -o /tmp/o.o
Iterate until clean.

HOW TO GET GROUND TRUTH
  # a deterministic mono/stereo source
  /workspace/executable -n -r 8000 -c 1 -b 16 /tmp/a.wav synth 0.01 sin 300
  # write your format and dump every byte
  /workspace/executable -D /tmp/a.wav /tmp/out.EXT && od -Ad -tx1z /tmp/out.EXT
  # read it back and confirm what the reference thinks it is
  /workspace/executable -V4 --i /tmp/out.EXT
  # round-trip the samples to text to check the codec
  /workspace/executable -D /tmp/out.EXT -t dat -
Vary channels, rates, encodings (-e/-b), lengths (including odd lengths that
need padding), and comments (--comment / --add-comment) so you see every header
field change. Also test writing to a PIPE ('-t EXT -' redirected to a file) --
non-seekable output usually changes what the writer can patch up afterwards, and
the reference may warn; reproduce that.
Test reading: hand-craft files with python3 to check the reader's tolerance and
error messages, e.g. truncated files, unknown chunks, wrong sizes.

FORMAT MODULE CONVENTIONS
 - One file per module: /workspace/src/fmt_<mod>.c exporting exactly
       sox_format_handler_t const *lsx_<mod>_format_fn(void);
   (the module list is /workspace/src/formats.h -- names are already fixed there)
 - Put '#define LSX_MODULE_NAME "<mod>"' at the very top before including
   "sox_i.h" so diagnostics read 'PROG WARN <mod>: ...'. Check the reference's
   actual subsystem name in its messages and match it.
 - handler.names lists the primary name first then aliases; handler.flags uses
   SOX_FILE_*; write_formats is a 0-terminated list of
   {encoding, bits..., 0, encoding, bits..., 0, 0} groups whose ORDER must match
   './executable --help-format <mod>' exactly. write_rates is a 0-terminated
   list of allowed rates or NULL.
 - Use the lsx_read*/lsx_write* helpers for endian-aware I/O and
   lsx_rawread/lsx_rawwrite for plain sample coding (declared in sox_i.h;
   another agent implements them).
 - Set ft->signal.rate/channels/length and ft->encoding.encoding/bits_per_sample
   in startread; set ft->signal.precision only if it is not derivable via
   lsx_precision().

Final message: a SHORT report (< 35 lines): which formats you implemented,
key layout facts, what remains uncertain, header additions.


YOUR ASSIGNMENT. Create these files under /workspace/src/ (and only these): fmt_wav.c adpcm.c ima_rw.c

Implement src/fmt_wav.c (the 'wav' handler, also named 'wavpcm' and
'amb'), plus shared ADPCM helpers in src/adpcm.c and src/ima_rw.c (declare their
interfaces in sox_i.h).

Reference facts to reproduce (verify all of them):
 - './executable --help-format wav' says:
     Description: Microsoft audio format ; Also handles: wavpcm amb
     Writes: 16/24/32-bit Signed Integer PCM, 8-bit Unsigned Integer PCM,
             8-bit u-law, 8-bit A-law, 4-bit MS ADPCM, 4-bit IMA ADPCM,
             32/64-bit Floating Point PCM   (in exactly that order)
 - A minimal 8000 Hz mono 16-bit write produces exactly:
     "RIFF" <size> "WAVE" "fmt " 16 <PCM=1> <ch> <rate> <byterate> <align>
     <bits> "data" <size> <samples...>
   (verified). Determine when the writer emits a 18-byte or 40-byte fmt chunk
   (WAVE_FORMAT_EXTENSIBLE), a 'fact' chunk, and the extra fields for the ADPCM
   encodings, plus padding of odd-sized chunks.
 - The 'amb' name selects B-format ambisonic WAV: determine what differs.
 - 'wavpcm' forces plain PCM: determine what differs.
 - RIFX (big-endian RIFF) must be READ (the reference lists no separate handler
   but 'soxformat.7' mentions it -- check by hand-crafting a RIFX file).
 - Reading: handle unknown chunks, LIST/INFO comments (write them too if the
   reference does -- check with --comment), 'fact' sample counts, cue points,
   and the --ignore-length option.
 - MS ADPCM and IMA ADPCM must be bit-exact both ways. Derive the codecs from
   round-trips: write a known ramp/sine to '-e ms-adpcm' and '-e ima-adpcm',
   dump the bytes, then read them back to -t dat. The block size chosen by the
   writer for a given rate/channels is observable in the fmt chunk; reproduce it.
 - GSM: the reference accepts '-e gsm-full-rate' per its -h text. Check whether
   'wav' can actually write it ('./executable a.wav -e gsm-full-rate out.wav');
   if it fails, reproduce the failure; if it works, implement GSM 06.10 -- report
   which.
Write findings to /workspace/notes/fmt_wav.md.

1	# Implementation contract
2	
3	This project is an original from-scratch re-implementation of the audio tool in
4	`/workspace/executable` (a build of "SoX v14.4.2").  Behaviour must be
5	discovered **only** by running `/workspace/executable`.  Never look for or use
6	the upstream source code, never decompile/disassemble/strace the binary.
7	
8	## Build
9	
10	`compile.sh` compiles every `src/**/*.c` into `./executable`.  Just add new `.c`
11	files under `src/`; no build file edits needed.  Compile with:
12	
13	    bash /workspace/compile.sh
14	
15	## Language / style
16	
17	* C99, no external libraries other than libm and libpthread.
18	* `#include "sox_i.h"` gives you everything (it includes `sox.h`).
19	* Internal linkage for everything except the one exported symbol per module.
20	
21	## Formats
22	
23	Each format module `src/<mod>.c` exports exactly:
24	
25	    sox_format_handler_t const *lsx_<mod>_format_fn(void);
26	
27	The module name list lives in `src/formats.h`.  A module may return a handler
28	whose `names` array lists the primary name first then aliases, e.g.
29	`{"aiff", "aif", NULL}`.
30	
31	Use the `lsx_read*/lsx_write*` helpers from `sox_i.h` for endian-aware I/O
32	(they honour `ft->encoding.reverse_bytes`).  Use `lsx_rawread`/`lsx_rawwrite`
33	for the actual sample coding once the header is dealt with.
34	
35	## Effects
36	
37	Each effect module `src/<eff>.c` exports exactly:
38	
39	    sox_effect_handler_t const *lsx_<eff>_effect_fn(void);
40	
41	The effect name list (and table order, which the reference's `-h` output
42	depends on) lives in `src/effects.h`.
43	
44	`effp->priv` is pre-allocated with `handler.priv_size` bytes, zeroed.
45	`getopts` receives `argc`/`argv` where `argv[0]` is *not* the effect name (the
46	first option is `argv[0]`), matching `lsx_getopt_init(argc, argv, ..., 0, &optstate)`
47	usage.  Return `lsx_usage(effp)` for a usage error.
48	
49	`flow` is invoked per-channel-group: unless the handler sets `SOX_EFF_MCHAN`,
50	the engine instantiates `effp->flows == in_signal.channels` copies and each
51	sees single-channel data.  With `SOX_EFF_MCHAN` there is one instance which
52	sees interleaved data.
53	
54	## Verifying
55	
56	`bash /workspace/compare.sh <args...>` runs the reference and our build with the
57	same arguments and diffs stdout, stderr, exit status and any produced file
58	byte-for-byte.  Use it constantly.
59	
60	Every message the reference prints must be reproduced exactly, including
61	`sox: ` / `sox WARN foo: ` prefixes and trailing punctuation.  Note the
62	reference prints its own `argv[0]` in messages; our build must print its own.

#!/bin/bash
# compare.sh -- run the reference and our build with identical arguments and
# report any difference in stdout, stderr, exit status or produced files.
#
# Usage: compare.sh [args...]
#   Any argument containing the token @@ is treated as an output file path;
#   @@ is replaced by a per-run scratch directory so the two runs cannot
#   collide, and the resulting files are compared byte-for-byte.
REF=${REF:-/workspace/executable}
OURS=${OURS:-/workspace/executable.new}
[ -x "$OURS" ] || OURS=/workspace/executable.mine

TMP=$(mktemp -d)
mkdir -p "$TMP/a" "$TMP/b"

argsA=(); argsB=()
for a in "$@"; do
  argsA+=("${a//@@/$TMP/a}")
  argsB+=("${a//@@/$TMP/b}")
done

"$REF"  "${argsA[@]}" >"$TMP/a.out" 2>"$TMP/a.err"; sa=$?
"$OURS" "${argsB[@]}" >"$TMP/b.out" 2>"$TMP/b.err"; sb=$?

# Normalise the program name that appears in diagnostics.
sed -i "s|$REF|SOX|g;s|$TMP/a|DIR|g" "$TMP/a.out" "$TMP/a.err"
sed -i "s|$OURS|SOX|g;s|$TMP/b|DIR|g" "$TMP/b.out" "$TMP/b.err"

rc=0
if [ "$sa" != "$sb" ]; then echo "EXIT: ref=$sa ours=$sb"; rc=1; fi
if ! diff -u "$TMP/a.out" "$TMP/b.out" >"$TMP/d1"; then
  echo "--- stdout differs"; cat "$TMP/d1"; rc=1
fi
if ! diff -u "$TMP/a.err" "$TMP/b.err" >"$TMP/d2"; then
  echo "--- stderr differs"; cat "$TMP/d2"; rc=1
fi
if ! diff -r "$TMP/a" "$TMP/b" >"$TMP/d3" 2>&1; then
  echo "--- output files differ"; cat "$TMP/d3"
  for f in "$TMP"/a/*; do
    b="$TMP/b/$(basename "$f")"
    [ -f "$b" ] || continue
    cmp -l "$f" "$b" | head -20
  done
  rc=1
fi
[ $rc = 0 ] && echo OK
rm -rf "$TMP"
exit $rc

# `formats_i.c` — low-level file I/O helpers

All behaviour below was determined by running `/workspace/executable`.

## The `lsx_check_read_params` diagnostics

A format's `startread` calls

```c
lsx_check_read_params(ft, channels, rate, encoding, bits_per_sample,
                      num_samples, check_length);
```

after decoding its header.  The reference emits these messages (all at **WARN**
level, and — because the code lives in `formats_i.c` — with the subsystem
prefix `formats_i`, e.g. `sox WARN formats_i: `foo.au': overriding sample
rate`).  `%s` is `ft->filename` exactly as it appeared on the command line
(`-` for stdin).  They are emitted in this order:

| condition | text |
|---|---|
| user `-c N` differs from header | ``` `%s': overriding number of channels ``` |
| user `-r N` differs from header | ``` `%s': overriding sample rate ``` |
| user `-e ENC` differs from header | ``` `%s': overriding encoding type ``` |
| user `-b N` differs from header | ``` `%s': overriding encoding size ``` |
| header length != length implied by file size | ``` `%s': file header gives the total number of samples as %llu but file length indicates the number is in fact %llu ``` |

Reproduce with e.g.

    sox -V4 -r 9000 -c 3 -b 8 -e unsigned-integer file.au -n stat

Formats observed to route through this function: `au`, `aiff`, `aifc`,
`sph`, `htk`, `sf`, `sndt`, `wve`.  `wav`, `voc`, `avr`, `smp`, `maud`, `dat`,
`txw` print their own (differently worded, mostly INFO-level) messages and must
**not** call it; `raw`-based types print `Format options overriding ...` from
`raw.c`.

### Semantics derived from experiment

* For each of the four fields: if the header value is non-zero *and* the
  `ft->signal`/`ft->encoding` field is already non-zero *and* they differ, warn
  and keep the user's value; **otherwise assign the header value**.  The
  "otherwise" branch assigns even when the header value is 0, which is how a
  header with `channels == 0` clobbers a user's `-c 3` (`formats.c` then
  reports `can't set 3 channels; using 1`) and how a header with `rate == 0`
  turns into `bad input format ...: sample rate zero or negative`.
* The file-size-derived sample count is
  `(lsx_filelength(ft) - lsx_tell(ft)) * 8 / bits_per_sample`, using the
  **header's** `bits_per_sample` argument, not the user's `-b` override
  (verified: `-b 8` and `-b 32` on a truncated 16-bit `.au` both report the
  same "in fact 978").  It is *not* rounded to whole frames (a stereo file with
  an odd byte count reports an odd number).
* The length check only runs when the file is seekable (real pipes never warn),
  when `check_length` is true, and when the header count is known.  A
  calculated value of 0 still warns ("... is in fact 0").
* The warning does **not** change `ft->signal.length`; the header's value is
  kept (`Duration` keeps showing the header figure).
* With `--ignore-length` the warning is suppressed and `ft->signal.length`
  becomes the calculated value instead (a real pipe then reports no
  `Duration` at all, i.e. length 0).  "Ignore length" is detected as
  `ft->ignore_length || ft->signal.length == SOX_IGNORE_LENGTH`.
* The function always returns `SOX_SUCCESS`; it performs no validation
  (`rate == 0` is diagnosed later, by `formats.c`).
* As a convenience it fills in `ft->signal.precision` from
  `lsx_precision(encoding, bits)` **only if it is still 0**.

## Conventions for the other helpers (for other modules' authors)

* `reverse_bytes == SOX_OPTION_YES` means "swap relative to the host".  Any
  other value (including `SOX_OPTION_DEFAULT`) means "host order", i.e. little
  endian here.
* `lsx_reads(ft, buf, len)` stores **at most `len` characters** and then always
  appends a NUL, so `buf` must hold `len + 1` bytes.  A NUL or a `\n`
  terminates the string and is consumed but not stored.  Returns `SOX_EOF` if
  the file ended before a terminator was seen (the partial string is still
  NUL-terminated).
* `lsx_readchars` reads exactly `len` bytes and appends nothing.
* `lsx_tell` returns `ftello` for seekable files, else the byte counter
  `ft->tell_off` maintained by `lsx_readbuf`/`lsx_writebuf`/`lsx_unreadb`.
* `lsx_seeki` on a non-seekable stream succeeds for `SEEK_CUR` with a
  non-negative offset (bytes are read and discarded) and otherwise fails with
  `SOX_EOF`, setting `ft->sox_errno`/`ft->sox_errstr`.
* `lsx_offset_seek(ft, byte_offset, to_sample)` rounds `to_sample` (a count over
  *all* channels) down to a whole frame and seeks to
  `byte_offset + to_sample_rounded * bits_per_sample / 8`.
* `lsx_filelength` returns 0 unless the underlying fd is a regular file.

### `lsx_read_fields`

Not present in any observable reference message, so its design is ours:

```c
int lsx_read_fields(sox_format_t ft, size_t *n, char const *spec, ...);
```

Scans whitespace-separated fields straight out of the file, consuming no more
input than necessary (one byte of pushback via `ungetc` is used), so it is safe
on a textual header that is followed by binary data.

* `*n` (may be NULL) receives the number of fields **assigned**.
* Returns `SOX_SUCCESS` only if every directive in `spec` was satisfied,
  otherwise `SOX_EOF`.
* Whitespace in `spec` matches a run of zero or more whitespace characters;
  any other literal character must match exactly.
* Conversions: `%d %i %u %o %x %X` (`h`, `hh`, `l`, `ll` modifiers; `0x`
  prefix accepted for `x`/`i`), `%f %e %g` (`float *`, or `double *` with
  `l`/`L`), `%s` (whitespace-delimited, NUL-terminated), `%c` (exactly
  `width` raw characters, default 1, no NUL, no whitespace skipping), `%%`,
  a field width, and `*` to suppress assignment.  Scan sets (`%[...]`) are
  **not** supported.

## Output encoding selection (verified over a large matrix)

Let `P` = the *input* signal's precision (before any effects).  Then:

1. If the user gave both `-e` and `-b` and the handler supports the combination,
   use it.
2. If the user gave `-e` only: restrict candidates to that encoding.
   If the user gave `-b` only: restrict candidates to that bit-width.
   (`-e signed-integer -b 12` on `wav` is unsupported, so the `-b` is dropped
   and the encoding-restricted search runs: with P=24 it yields 24-bit.)
3. Among the handler's `write_formats` list, in list order, pick the entry with
   the *smallest* precision that is >= P, and when several have equal precision
   pick the **last** such entry.  If the input's own encoding appears anywhere in
   the list, restrict the search to that encoding first (this is why u-law input
   to `wav` gives u-law and not MS-ADPCM, both precision 14).
4. If no entry reaches P, pick the entry with the greatest precision, ties going
   to the **first** such entry (u-law input, P=14, to `prc` whose candidates are
   A-law/8 and IMA-ADPCM/4, both precision 13, gives A-law).

## Auto-inserted effects

The chain is: `input`, then all user effects in order, then (if needed)
`channels`, then `rate`, then `dither`, then `output`.  Verified: the auto
`rate`/`channels` always come *after* every user effect, even a user `rate`.

`dither` is inserted when the running precision exceeds the output encoding's
precision and dithering is not disabled (`-D`).  Running precision is computed
by `sox_add_effect` as: unchanged when the handler has `SOX_EFF_MODIFY`
(meaning "does not modify samples"), self-computed when it has `SOX_EFF_PREC`,
otherwise `SOX_SAMPLE_PRECISION` (32).  Observed consequences:

* `st.wav -t s16 -c 4 out` — no dither (channels *up*-mix keeps precision).
* `st.wav -t s16 -c 1 out` — dither (down-mix raises precision).
* `st.wav -t s16 out reverse` — no dither (`reverse` has SOX_EFF_MODIFY).
* `-m` (mix) — dither; `-M` (merge) — no dither.
* float output — never dithered.

`-G`/`--guard` prepends a `gain` effect (`gain -h`); `--norm` = guard +
normalise, which runs the chain into a temporary file and then a second pass.

## Miscellaneous

* Format options must precede their file name.  Anything after the first
  recognised effect name is effect arguments; a stray `-t wav name` there is a
  usage error (banner + full usage, exit 1).
* An unrecognised word where an effect is expected is treated as a *file name*.
* `-n -n` (null input and null output) hangs — never test that.
* Default `--buffer` is 8192.
* Default output comment is `Processed by SoX`.

.B .amb
Ambisonic B-Format: a specialisation of

with between 3 and 16 channels of audio for use with an Ambisonic decoder.
See http://www.ambisonia.com/Members/mleese/file-format-for-b-format for
details.  It is up to the user to get the channels together in the right
order and at the correct amplitude.
.TP
\&\fB.amr\-nb\fR (optional)
Adaptive Multi Rate\*mNarrow Band speech codec; a lossy format used in 3rd
generation mobile telephony and defined in 3GPP TS 26.071 et al.
.SP
AMR-NB audio has a fixed sampling rate of 8 kHz and supports encoding
passing the decoded audio through a high-pass filter, e.g.:
.EX
	sox input.vox output.wav highpass 10
.EE
.TP
\&\fB.w64\fR (optional)
Sonic Foundry's 64-bit RIFF/WAV format.
.TP
\&\fB.wav\fR (also with \fB\-t sndfile\fR)
Microsoft .WAV RIFF files.
This is the native audio file format of Windows, and widely used for uncompressed audio.
.SP
Normally \fB.wav\fR files have all formatting information
in their headers, and so do not need any format options
specified for an input file.  If any are, they will
override the file header, and you will be warned to this effect.
You had better know what you are doing! Output format
options will cause a format conversion, and the \fB.wav\fR
will written appropriately.
.SP
SoX can read and write linear PCM, floating point, \(*m-law, A-law, MS ADPCM, and IMA (or DVI) ADPCM encoded samples.
WAV files can also contain audio encoded in many other ways (not currently
supported with SoX) e.g. MP3; in some cases such a file can still be
read by SoX by overriding the file type, e.g.
.EX
   play \-t mp3 mp3\-encoded.wav
.EE
Big endian versions of RIFF files, called RIFX, are also supported.
To write a RIFX file, use the
.B \-B
option with the output file options.
.TP
\fBwaveaudio\fR (optional)
MS-Windows native audio device driver.  Examples:
.EX
	sox infile \-t waveaudio
	sox infile \-t waveaudio default
	sox infile \-t waveaudio 1
	sox infile \-t waveaudio "High Definition Audio Device ("
.EE
If the device name is omitted, \fB-1\fR, or \fBdefault\fR, then you
get the `Microsoft Wave Mapper' device.  Wave Mapper means `use the
system default audio devices'.  You can control what `default' means
via the OS Control Panel.
.SP
If the device name given is some other number, you get that audio
device by index; so recording with device name \fB0\fR would get the
first input device (perhaps the microphone), \fB1\fR would get the
second (perhaps line in), etc.  Playback using \fB0\fR will get the
first output device (usually the only audio device).
.SP
If the device name given is something other than a number, SoX tries
to match it (maximum 31 characters) against the names of the available
devices.
.SP
See also
.BR play (1),
.BR rec (1),
and
.BR sox (1)
.BR \-d .
.TP
.B .wavpcm
A non-standard, but widely used, variant of
.BR .wav .
Some applications cannot read a standard WAV file header for PCM-encoded
data with sample-size greater than 16-bits or with more than two
channels, but can read a non-standard
WAV header.  It is likely that such applications will eventually be
updated to support the standard header, but in the mean time, this SoX
format can be used to create files with the non-standard header that
should work with these applications.  (Note that SoX will automatically
detect and read WAV files with the non-standard header.)
.SP
The most common use of this file-type is likely to be along the following
lines:
.EX
	sox infile.any \-t wavpcm \-e signed-integer outfile.wav
.EE
